pitfalls: Writing $x\overline{y} + y\overline{z}$ with two NOT gates, which the question forbids.
cse-2002-b-55-a.verification: Rows where $f = 1$: $xy' = 1$ at 100, 101; $yz' = 1$ at 010, 110. $(x + y)(yz)'$ is 1 at 010, 100, 101, 110 and 0 elsewhere (at 011 and 111, $yz = 1$). Same four rows.

cse-2002-b-55-b.approach: Concept tested: **multi-level NAND conversion by bubble pairs**. The circuit is AND → OR → OR; the first AND–OR level becomes NAND–NAND, and the second OR level needs an inverter (an unpaired bubble) before it can be a NAND too.

steps.title: Read the circuit
steps.body: $f = (ab + cd) + ef$: AND gates on $(a, b)$, $(c, d)$, $(e, f)$, an OR of the first two, and an OR of that with the third.

steps.title: First AND–OR level
steps.body: $N_1 = \overline{ab}$, $N_2 = \overline{cd}$, $N_3 = \overline{N_1 N_2} = ab + cd$ (NAND–NAND).

steps.title: The second OR level
steps.body: To NAND $ab + cd$ with $ef$, the output NAND needs both inputs complemented: $\overline{ef}$ comes from $N_5 = \overline{ef}$, and $\overline{ab + cd}$ needs an inverter $N_4 = \overline{N_3 N_3}$.

steps.title: Output
steps.body: $f = \overline{N_4 N_5} = \overline{N_4} + \overline{N_5} = (ab + cd) + ef$. Six 2-input NANDs: $N_1, \ldots, N_5$ and the output gate.

answer.value: N1 = (ab)′, N2 = (cd)′, N3 = NAND(N1, N2), N4 = NAND(N3, N3), N5 = (ef)′, f = NAND(N4, N5): six 2-input NANDs

cse-2002-b-55-b.shortcut: Draw every gate as NAND and count bubbles on each wire: wherever a wire has a single bubble (here between the two OR levels), add one inverter.
pitfalls: Replacing every gate by a NAND without the inverter, which computes $\overline{ab + cd} + ef$.
Using a 3-input NAND for the OR of three products (the question requires 2-input gates).

cse-2002-b-56-a.approach: Each falling edge shifts the data one stage down: R0 takes the new inputs, R1 the first-stage result of R0, R2 the second-stage result of R1. So after clock $k$, R2 holds pair $k-2$ and $Z$ (from the last full adder) is $A_{k-2}+B_{k-2}$.

steps.title: Stage timing
steps.body: Stage 1 (FA under R0) adds $a_0+b_0$ into R1; stage 2 adds $a_1+b_1+c_1$ into R2; stage 3 (FA under R2) is combinational and drives $z_3z_2$, with $z_1=s_1$, $z_0=s_0$ taken from R2. Hence $Z$ after clock $k$ is the sum of the pair loaded at clock $k-2$.

steps.title: Clocks 1–2: pipeline filling
steps.body: After clocks 1 and 2, R2 still holds its initial zeros, so $Z = 0+0 = 0000$ both times.

steps.title: Clocks 7–8
steps.body: R2 now holds pairs 5 and 6, both $000+000$, so $Z = 0000$ after clocks 7 and 8.

animation.caption: Contents after each falling edge (pair # loaded at that clock)

pitfalls: Producing $1011$ already after clock 1 — the result needs two more edges to reach R2.
Treating stage 3 as registered — $Z$ comes from a combinational full adder after R2.

cse-2002-b-56-b.approach: Read the data path: one full adder per bit position, carries passed down through registers, unused bits delayed alongside — a ripple-carry adder cut into stages by registers.

steps.title: Per-stage work
steps.body: Stage 1 adds bit 0 ($a_0+b_0+0$), stage 2 adds bit 1 with the carry from stage 1, stage 3 adds bit 2 with the carry from stage 2 and outputs the final carry $z_3$. Each carry travels to the next stage through a register.

steps.title: Why the extra register bits
steps.body: The higher bits ($a_2,b_2,a_1,b_1$) and the already computed sum bits ($s_0$, later $s_1$) are copied down unchanged so they stay aligned with their own operation. A new addition can start every clock; each result appears 2 clocks after its inputs are loaded (Z = 1011 after clock 3 for the pair loaded at clock 1).

answer.value: A 3-stage pipelined 3-bit (ripple-carry) binary adder: $Z = A + B$ (4-bit result), one addition per clock with a latency of 2 clocks

pitfalls: Calling it a serial adder — all three bit-additions of different operand pairs are in progress simultaneously.
cse-2002-b-56-b.verification: Part (a) gives $Z = A+B$ for every input pair, two clocks after loading.

cse-2002-b-57-a.approach: Concept tested: a **base-16** format with an **excess-64** exponent and an unusual field order (sign | fraction | exponent). Normalise so the first *hex digit* of the fraction is non-zero, then assemble the 32 bits and regroup into hex.
cse-2002-b-57-a.given:
| Field | Bits | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| sign (MSB) | 1 | 0 = +, 1 = − |
| fraction | 24 | point at its left end |
| exponent | 7 | excess-64, base 16 |

steps.title: Normalise in base 16
steps.body: Move the point one hex digit left: $7.8_{16} = 0.78_{16} \times 16^{1}$. The first hex digit (7) is non-zero, so this is normalised and $E = 1$.

cse-2002-b-57-a.shortcut: In base 16 a value between 1 and 16 always has exponent 1 (one hex digit before the point), so the exponent field is $64 + 1 = 41_{16}$ immediately.
pitfalls: Normalising in binary ($0.1111 \times 2^3$): the exponent is a power of 16, so normalise by hex digits.
Putting the exponent right after the sign, as in IEEE: this format puts it last.
Reading the fields' hex digits directly (`1 780000 41`): the fields are not nibble-aligned, so regroup the whole word.

cse-2002-b-57-b.approach: Concept tested: the **largest value** of a base-16 format. Take the largest fraction ($0.FFFFFF_{16}$) and the largest exponent (excess-64 in 7 bits gives $+63$), then convert $16^{63}$ to a power of 10.

steps.title: Largest fraction
steps.body: All 24 bits 1: $0.FFFFFF_{16} = 1 - 16^{-6} \approx 1$.

steps.title: Convert to a power of 10
steps.body: $\log_{10} 2^{252} = 252 \times 0.30103 \approx 75.86$, so $x_{\max} \approx 10^{75.86} \approx 7.2 \times 10^{75}$. The nearest power of 10 is $10^{76}$.

pitfalls: Using base 2 ($2^{63} \approx 10^{19}$): the exponent is a power of 16.
Taking $E_{\max} = 64$ or $127$: excess-64 in 7 bits reaches $+63$.
Rounding $10^{75.86}$ down to $10^{75}$: the nearest power is $10^{76}$.

cse-2002-b-58-a.approach: Map each element to its cache line: line $=\lfloor\text{address}/16\rfloor \bmod 512$. Two elements conflict only if they map to the same line but lie in different memory blocks.

steps.title: Cache geometry
steps.body: Lines $= 8\,\text{KB}/16\,\text{B} = 8192/16 = 512$. Element $A[i]$ is at byte address $4i$, in memory block $\lfloor4i/16\rfloor = \lfloor i/4\rfloor$ and cache line $\lfloor i/4\rfloor \bmod 512$.

steps.title: Who maps to line 0?
steps.body: $A[0]$ is in block 0, line 0. Another block maps to line 0 only if its block number is a multiple of 512, i.e. byte address $\ge 512\times16 = 8192$, i.e. $i \ge 2048$.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.body: The array is $2048\times4 = 8192$ bytes — exactly the cache size, so indices $0..2047$ occupy blocks $0..511$, each on its own line. **No element conflicts with $A[0]$.** $A[1], A[2], A[3]$ share line 0 with $A[0]$ but are in the same block, so they are brought in together rather than evicting it.

answer.value: None — the 8 KB array fits exactly in the 8 KB cache (blocks 0–511 map to distinct lines); $A[1..3]$ share $A[0]$’s block, so they do not conflict
answer.keyNote: The stored key ("Base address + 4 * 2048 = 8192 bytes = 2 pages of 4 KB each") does not name any conflicting element and talks about pages, which are irrelevant to cache mapping. The first element that would map to line 0 from a different block is at byte 8192, i.e. $A[2048]$, outside the array; so no element of the array conflicts with $A[0]$.

pitfalls: Calling $A[1..3]$ conflicts — same block means same tag, so they hit together.
Mixing pages (virtual memory) with cache lines.
cse-2002-b-58-a.verification: Total blocks in the array $= 8192/16 = 512 =$ number of cache lines, so the block-to-line map $b\mapsto b \bmod 512$ is one-to-one on the array.

cse-2002-b-58-b.approach: In a reverse sweep each 16-byte block (4 floats) misses once on its first-touched element; since the whole array fits in the cache without conflicts, nothing is evicted.

steps.title: Blocks touched
steps.body: Elements per block $=16/4 = 4$. Blocks in the array $= 2048/4 = 512$.

steps.title: Misses per block
steps.body: Going from $A[2047]$ down, the first access to a block (e.g. $A[2047]$ for block 511) misses and loads $A[2044..2047]$; the next 3 accesses hit. No eviction can occur because the 512 blocks map to 512 distinct lines (part a).

steps.title: Total
steps.body: Misses $= 512\text{ blocks}\times1 = 512$ (all compulsory); hits $= 2048-512 = 1536$.

answer.value: 512 misses (one compulsory miss per 16-byte block; no conflict misses)

pitfalls: Answering 2048 — that ignores that a 16-byte line brings in 4 elements at once.
cse-2002-b-58-b.verification: Direction does not matter for compulsory misses: forward order also gives $2048/4 = 512$.

cse-2002-b-59.approach: Read the parameters as move($n$, source, auxiliary, destination): the printf moves disk $n$ from A to C, so first park $n-1$ disks on B (using C), then bring them from B to C (using A).

steps.title: Base condition
steps.body: The body must run only while disks remain: `if (n > 0)`. For $n=0$ nothing is printed.

steps.title: First recursive call
steps.body: Before disk $n$ can go from A to C, the top $n-1$ disks must move from A to B using C as the spare: `move(n-1, A, C, B)` (source A, auxiliary C, destination B).

steps.title: Second recursive call

answer.value: `if (n > 0)`, `move(n-1, A, C, B)`, `move(n-1, B, A, C)`

pitfalls: Swapping the roles in the first call (`move(n-1, A, B, C)`) — that would put the $n-1$ disks on C, blocking disk $n$.
cse-2002-b-59.verification: $n=2$: prints "disk 1 A→B", "disk 2 A→C", "disk 1 B→C" — a valid 3-move solution ($2^2-1$).

cse-2002-b-60-a.approach: With unit edge weights, a direct edge gives path length 1 and a missing edge must start as "no path known", i.e. $\infty$, so that min() ignores it.

steps.title: No edge
steps.body: If $A[i,j]=0$ there is no direct path, so $P[i,j]$ must be $\infty$ (a value larger than any real path length, e.g. $n$ or more); using $0$ would make min() pick a non-existent path.

steps.title: Edge
steps.body: If $A[i,j]=1$ the direct edge is a path of length 1, so $P[i,j] = 1$ (equivalently $A[i,j]$).

pitfalls: Initialising missing edges to 0.
cse-2002-b-60-a.verification: After the algorithm, $P[i,j]$ is the minimum number of edges on an $i\to j$ path, and stays $\infty$ exactly when $j$ is unreachable from $i$.

cse-2002-b-60-b.approach: The outermost loop variable $i$ must be the intermediate vertex (Floyd–Warshall’s phase), so relax every pair $(j,k)$ through $i$.

steps.title: Identify the intermediate vertex
steps.body: Floyd–Warshall’s invariant: after phase $i$, $P[j,k]$ is the shortest $j\to k$ path using only intermediates from $\{1,\dots,i\}$. The phase variable must be the **outermost** loop, which here is $i$.

steps.title: Relaxation line
steps.body:
Inside, update every pair through vertex $i$:
$$P[j,k] = \min\{P[j,k],\ P[j,i] + P[i,k]\}$$

pitfalls: Writing $P[i,j] = \min\{P[i,j], P[i,k]+P[k,j]\}$ — with $k$ innermost this is not Floyd–Warshall and gives wrong results.

cse-2002-b-60-c.approach: Three nested loops of $n$ iterations each with constant work inside.

steps.title: Count iterations
steps.body: Loops over $i$, $j$, $k$ each run $n$ times, so the min() line runs $n\cdot n\cdot n = n^3$ times; each execution is $O(1)$.

steps.title: Initialisation
steps.body: The initialisation is $n^2$ steps, dominated by $n^3$. Total: $O(n^3)$.

cse-2002-b-61-a.approach: An ordered sum $n = x_1 + x_2$ is fixed once $x_1$ is chosen from $1..n-1$.

steps.title: Choose the first part
steps.body: $x_1 \ge 1$ and $x_2 = n - x_1 \ge 1 \Rightarrow 1 \le x_1 \le n-1$: $n-1$ choices, each giving a different ordered pair.

steps.title: Check
steps.body: $n=3$: $x_1\in\{1,2\}$ gives $1+2, 2+1$ — 2 ways, matching the example.

pitfalls: Counting unordered sums ($\lfloor n/2\rfloor$) — the example counts $1+2$ and $2+1$ separately.

cse-2002-b-61-b.approach: Stars and bars: place 2 dividers in the $n-1$ gaps between $n$ ones.

steps.title: Model
steps.body: Write $n$ as $1+1+\dots+1$; there are $n-1$ gaps between the ones. Choosing 2 distinct gaps for dividers splits them into 3 positive ordered parts, and every composition arises exactly once.

cse-2002-b-61-c.approach: Generalise stars and bars: $k$ positive parts need $k-1$ dividers in the $n-1$ gaps.

steps.title: Dividers
steps.body: Among the $n-1$ gaps between $n$ ones, choose $k-1$ for dividers; this yields $k$ non-empty ordered groups, i.e. $x_1+\dots+x_k = n$ with each $x_i\ge1$.

steps.title: Count
steps.body:
$$\binom{n-1}{k-1}$$
Checks: $k=2$ gives $n-1$ (part a); $k=3$ gives $\binom{n-1}{2}$ (part b).

pitfalls: Using $\binom{n+k-1}{k-1}$, which counts non-negative parts.
cse-2002-b-61-c.verification: Substituting $y_i = x_i-1\ge0$: $\sum y_i = n-k$, with $\binom{(n-k)+k-1}{k-1} = \binom{n-1}{k-1}$ solutions.

cse-2002-b-62-a.approach: Build $M$ (from $\langle M',x\rangle$) so its input is irrelevant: it discards $w$ and runs $M'$ on the hard-wired $x$.

steps.title: Construction
steps.body: $M$ has $M'$ and $x$ built into its states. On input $w$, it first **erases $w$, writes $x$ on the tape and simulates $M'$ on $x$**.

steps.title: Why ignore w
steps.body: The target language demands "halts and outputs 1 **irrespective of the input**"; making $M$’s behaviour independent of $w$ turns that "for all inputs" condition into a single question: does $M'$ halt on $x$?

answer.value: Ignore (erase) $w$, write $x$ on the tape and simulate $M'$ on $x$

cse-2002-b-62-a.verification: This is the standard reduction from HALT; the map $\langle M',x\rangle\mapsto M$ is computable since it only writes out a fixed program around $M'$ and $x$.

cse-2002-b-62-b.approach: If the simulation finishes, output 1 and halt; if it never finishes, $M$ never halts.

steps.title: Second step
steps.body: If the simulation of $M'$ on $x$ halts (whatever $M'$ outputs), $M$ **writes 1 on its tape and halts**. If $M'$ runs forever on $x$, the simulation never ends and $M$ never halts.

steps.title: Resulting property
steps.body: So $M$ halts with output 1 on every $w$ $\iff$ $M'$ halts on $x$. A decider for the target language would decide HALT, which is impossible — hence the language is undecidable.

answer.value: If the simulation of $M'$ on $x$ halts, $M$ outputs 1 and halts (otherwise it runs forever)

pitfalls: Outputting $M'$’s own result — it must be 1 regardless of what $M'$ outputs.
cse-2002-b-62-b.verification: Both directions: $M'$ halts on $x$ ⇒ $M$ outputs 1 on all $w$; $M'$ loops on $x$ ⇒ $M$ halts on no $w$.

cse-2002-b-62-c.approach: Reduce HALT $\le$ L: from $\langle M',x\rangle$ build $M$ that ignores its own input $w$, runs $M'$ on the hard-wired $x$, and prints 1 if that run halts. Then $M$'s behaviour is the same on every $w$, and it is "halt and output 1" exactly when $M'$ halts on $x$.

steps.title: Construction of M (parts a, b)
steps.body:
Given $\langle M', xangle$, the reduction outputs a machine $M$ that, on input $w$:

1. erases $w$ and writes the fixed string $x$ on its tape (step a);
2. simulates $M'$ on $x$; if the simulation halts, $M$ erases the tape, writes $1$ and halts (step b).

This is a purely syntactic transformation of $\langle M', xangle$, so it is computable (and always terminates).

steps.title: Key property (part c)
steps.body:
Because $M$ discards $w$, its run is identical for every $w$:

- if $M'$ halts on $x$ $\Rightarrow$ $M$ halts with output $1$ on **every** $w$, so $\langle Mangle \in L$;
- if $M'$ does not halt on $x$ $\Rightarrow$ $M$ runs forever on **every** $w$, so $\langle Mangle 
otin L$.

Hence $\langle Mangle \in L \iff M'$ halts on $x$.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.body: If $L$ were decidable, deciding $\langle M\rangle \in L$ would decide whether $M'$ halts on $x$ — the halting problem, which is undecidable. So $L$ is undecidable.

answer.value: $M$ halts and outputs 1 on every input $w$ **iff** $M'$ halts on $x$ (and $M$ behaves identically on all $w$, since it ignores $w$).

pitfalls: Letting $M$ actually use $w$ — then its behaviour can depend on the input and the "irrespective of input" property breaks.
Reducing in the wrong direction (L to HALT proves nothing about L).
cse-2002-b-62-c.verification: Checked both cases: halting run gives output 1 for all $w$; non-halting run gives no output for any $w$.

cse-2002-b-63-a-i.approach: Take the roll numbers that appear in INTERVIEW, subtract those that appear in OFFER, then join with STUDENT to pick up the names.
cse-2002-b-63-a-i.given:
| Relation | Key |
|---|---|
| STUDENT(srollno, sname, sdegree) | srollno |
| INTERVIEW(cname, srollno, idate) | (cname, srollno) |
| OFFER(cname, srollno, osalary) | (cname, srollno) |

steps.title: Interviewed students
steps.body: $\pi_{srollno}(\text{INTERVIEW})$ = roll numbers of students who attended at least one interview.

steps.title: Remove those with an offer
steps.body: $\pi_{srollno}(\text{INTERVIEW}) - \pi_{srollno}(\text{OFFER})$ keeps exactly the roll numbers that have **no** tuple in OFFER, i.e. no job offer at all. Both operands are single-column on srollno, so the difference is union-compatible.

steps.title: Attach names
steps.body: Join with STUDENT on srollno and project:\n\n$$\pi_{srollno,\,sname}\big(\text{STUDENT} \bowtie (\pi_{srollno}(\text{INTERVIEW}) - \pi_{srollno}(\text{OFFER}))\big)$$

pitfalls: Subtracting before projecting: $\text{INTERVIEW} - \text{OFFER}$ is not union-compatible (idate vs osalary).
Using STUDENT − OFFER also returns students who never interviewed.
cse-2002-b-63-a-i.verification: A student with interviews but zero offers survives the difference; any student with one or more offers is removed.

cse-2002-b-63-a-ii.approach: "Offer from every company interviewed with" = interviewed and **no** (company, student) interview pair is missing from OFFER. Find the missing pairs with a difference on (cname, srollno), and remove those students.
cse-2002-b-63-a-ii.given:
| Relation | Key |
|---|---|
| STUDENT(srollno, sname, sdegree) | srollno |
| INTERVIEW(cname, srollno, idate) | (cname, srollno) |
| OFFER(cname, srollno, osalary) | (cname, srollno) |

steps.title: Interviews without an offer
steps.body: $X = \pi_{cname,srollno}(\text{INTERVIEW}) - \pi_{cname,srollno}(\text{OFFER})$ lists every (company, student) interview that did **not** produce an offer.

steps.title: Students with no such pair
steps.body: $\pi_{srollno}(\text{INTERVIEW}) - \pi_{srollno}(X)$ = students who interviewed and for whom every interview yielded an offer.

steps.title: Attach names
steps.body: $$\pi_{srollno,\,sname}\Big(\text{STUDENT} \bowtie \big(\pi_{srollno}(\text{INTERVIEW}) - \pi_{srollno}(\pi_{cname,srollno}(\text{INTERVIEW}) - \pi_{cname,srollno}(\text{OFFER}))\big)\Big)$$

pitfalls: Starting from STUDENT instead of INTERVIEW would include students who never interviewed (vacuously "every company").
Division by all companies is wrong — only the companies the student interviewed with matter.
cse-2002-b-63-a-ii.verification: Student interviewed by C1, C2 with offers from both: no pair in X, kept. Offer only from C1: (C2, s) in X, removed.

cse-2002-b-63-b.approach: Join STUDENT with OFFER, group by degree, keep groups with more than five distinct offered students, and output the degree with AVG(osalary).

steps.title: Join offers to degrees
steps.body: OFFER has no degree, so join `STUDENT S, OFFER O WHERE S.srollno = O.srollno`; each row is one offer with the student's degree.

steps.title: Group and filter
steps.body: `GROUP BY S.sdegree` forms one group per degree. A student can hold several offers, so count students with `COUNT(DISTINCT S.srollno) > 5` in `HAVING` (a WHERE clause cannot use aggregates).

steps.title: Query
steps.body:
```sql
SELECT S.sdegree, AVG(O.osalary)
FROM STUDENT S, OFFER O
WHERE S.srollno = O.srollno
GROUP BY S.sdegree
HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT S.srollno) > 5;
```

answer.value: `SELECT S.sdegree, AVG(O.osalary) FROM STUDENT S, OFFER O WHERE S.srollno = O.srollno GROUP BY S.sdegree HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT S.srollno) > 5`

pitfalls: `COUNT(*) > 5` counts offers, not students — a student with two offers would be counted twice.
Putting the count condition in WHERE is illegal; aggregates go in HAVING.
cse-2002-b-63-b.verification: Degree with 6 students holding 9 offers passes (6 > 5); degree with 3 students holding 8 offers is rejected, which COUNT(*) would wrongly accept.

cse-2002-b-64-a.approach: Binary decomposition test: lossless iff $R_1\cap R_2$ is a superkey of $R_1$ or of $R_2$.

cse-2002-b-64-c.given: $R(L,M,N,O,P)$, $F=\{M\to O,\ NO\to P,\ P\to L,\ L\to MN\}$, $R_1=(L,M,N,P)$, $R_2=(M,O)$.

cse-2002-b-65-a.approach: In a B-tree keys live in internal nodes too, so a hit can stop at any level; a miss always reaches a leaf. In a B+-tree every search, hit or miss, goes root-to-leaf, and all leaves are at the same depth.

steps.title: B-tree
steps.body: Successful: the key may be found at the root, an internal node or a leaf, so the number of levels visited depends on the key — $X_1$ = **Variable**. Unsuccessful: the search must descend to a leaf (height $h$, same for all leaves) before failing — $X_2$ = **Constant**.

steps.title: B+-tree
steps.body: Internal nodes hold only routing copies; records/keys are in the leaves. Every search follows one root-to-leaf path of length $h$, whether or not it finds the key — $X_3$ = $X_4$ = **Constant**.

pitfalls: Treating a match against a B+-tree routing key in an internal node as a successful search — the data is only at the leaf.
cse-2002-b-65-a.verification: B-tree of height 3 with key k at root: 1 node read; key in a leaf: 3 reads. Missing key: always 3. B+-tree: always 3.

cse-2002-b-66-a.approach: With non-preemptive scheduling a running process leaves the CPU only by blocking or exiting, so the usual running → ready (time-out / preemption) arc is absent.

steps.title: Transitions
steps.body:
| From | To | Label |
|---|---|---|
| created | ready | admitted |
| ready | running | dispatched by scheduler |
| running | blocked | waits for I/O / event |
| blocked | ready | I/O / event completes |
| running | terminated | exit |

steps.title: Missing arc
steps.body: There is **no running → ready** edge: no timer interrupt or higher-priority arrival can take the CPU away. Also blocked → running is not allowed (a woken process must be dispatched from ready).

answer.value: created →(admit) ready →(dispatch) running; running →(I/O or event wait) blocked →(event completion) ready; running →(exit) terminated; no running → ready transition.

pitfalls: Drawing a running → ready (time-slice expiry) arc — that only exists with preemption.
cse-2002-b-66-a.verification: Every exit from running is voluntary (block or terminate), which is exactly non-preemptive behaviour.

cse-2002-b-66-b-i.approach: TEST-AND-SET returns the old value and sets the lock to 1. Spin while the old value was 1 (someone inside); release by writing 0.

steps.title: Entry
Exit
steps.body: Setting `mutex = 0` lets exactly one spinning process see 0 on its next TEST-AND-SET.

pitfalls: Writing `while (!TEST-AND-SET(&mutex))` — that spins exactly when the lock is free.
cse-2002-b-66-b-i.verification: Two processes: first gets 0 and enters, the second gets 1 until the first writes 0.

cse-2002-b-66-b-ii.approach: Check progress (some waiter always gets in) and bounded waiting (each waiter eventually gets in) for the plain TAS spinlock.

steps.title: Deadlock-free: yes
steps.body: When the CS is free, mutex = 0, so the first TEST-AND-SET executed by any waiting process returns 0 and that process enters. Processes can never all wait forever with the lock free.

steps.title: Starvation-free: no
steps.body: There is no ordering among spinners. When P1 leaves and sets mutex = 0, P2 may grab it before P3 every single time; P3 can lose the race indefinitely. No bounded-waiting guarantee.

pitfalls: Assuming mutual exclusion + progress implies bounded waiting.
cse-2002-b-66-b-ii.verification: Schedule P2 → P3(fails) → P2 exit → P2 re-enter → P3(fails)… repeats forever with P3 never entering.

cse-2002-b-66-b-iii.approach: Interleave two processes between A1 (read) and A2 (write) while mutex = 0: both read 0 before either writes 1.

steps.title: Result
steps.body: Both calls return 0, so both `while` loops exit and P1 and P2 are inside the critical section together — mutual exclusion is violated.

answer.value: P1 executes A1 (y = 0), then P2 executes A1 (y = 0) before P1 executes A2; both then execute A2 and A3, both return 0 and both enter the critical section.

pitfalls: Interleaving after A2 of the first process — then the second process reads 1 and the race does not occur.
cse-2002-b-66-b-iii.verification: The bad window is exactly between A1 and A2 of a process; the example places P2's A1 inside it.

cse-2002-b-67-a.approach: Offset = $\log_2 4096 = 12$ bits; the remaining 20 page-number bits split equally, 10 + 10. Each level indexes a 1024-entry table that fits exactly in one page.
cse-2002-b-67-a.given:
| Item | Value |
|---|---|
| Virtual / physical address | 32 bits / 32 bits |
| Page size | 4 KB |
| PTE size | 4 bytes |
| Levels | 2, equal index bits |

steps.title: Address split
steps.body: Offset: $4\text{ KB}=2^{12}$ B $\Rightarrow 12$ bits. Page number: $32-12=20$ bits $\Rightarrow$ $p_1$ = 10 bits, $p_2$ = 10 bits.

steps.title: Translation path
steps.body: 1. Page-table base register (PTBR) $+\ 4\cdot p_1$ $\to$ level-1 entry, which holds the frame of the level-2 table.\n2. That frame base $+\ 4\cdot p_2$ $\to$ level-2 entry, which holds the 20-bit frame number $f$.\n3. Physical address = $f$ (20 bits) concatenated with the 12-bit offset $d$: $PA = f\cdot 2^{12}+d$.

steps.title: Why 10 bits fit
steps.body: $2^{10}$ entries $\times 4$ B $= 4096$ B $=$ one page, so every page table (outer or inner) occupies exactly one frame.

answer.value: VA = $p_1$ (10 bits) | $p_2$ (10 bits) | $d$ (12 bits). PTBR + $p_1$ selects the level-1 entry → base of a level-2 table; + $p_2$ selects the level-2 entry → 20-bit frame number $f$; PA = $f$ ∥ $d$.

pitfalls: Translating the offset — it is copied unchanged into the physical address.
cse-2002-b-67-a.verification: $10+10+12=32$ bits for VA; $20+12=32$ bits for PA.

cse-2002-b-67-b.approach: Entries per page = page size ÷ PTE size.
cse-2002-b-67-b.given:
| Item | Value |
|---|---|
| Virtual / physical address | 32 bits / 32 bits |
| Page size | 4 KB |
| PTE size | 4 bytes |
| Levels | 2, equal index bits |

steps.title: Divide
steps.body: $\dfrac{4\text{ KB}}{4\text{ B}} = \dfrac{4096}{4} = 1024 = 2^{10}$ entries.

steps.title: Consistency
steps.body: This matches the 10-bit index used at each level, so each page table occupies exactly one page.

pitfalls: Using 4 bits instead of 4 bytes for the entry size.

cse-2002-b-67-c.approach: A PTE must hold a frame number; whatever is left of its 32 bits is free for protection, valid, dirty and similar bits.
cse-2002-b-67-c.given:
| Item | Value |
|---|---|
| Virtual / physical address | 32 bits / 32 bits |
| Page size | 4 KB |
| PTE size | 4 bytes |
| Levels | 2, equal index bits |

steps.title: Frame number width
steps.body: Frames $=\dfrac{2^{32}}{2^{12}}=2^{20}$ $\Rightarrow$ frame number = 20 bits. (Page tables themselves are page-aligned, so level-1 entries also need only 20 bits.)

steps.title: Spare bits
steps.body: PTE = 4 B = 32 bits $\Rightarrow 32-20=12$ bits for protection and other information.

pitfalls: Subtracting the 10-bit index instead of the 20-bit frame number.

cse-2002-b-68-a.approach: b_empty counts free slots (initially BUFFSIZE), b_full counts filled slots (initially 0). Wait on the resource you need, signal the one you create.

steps.title: Producer
steps.body: Before writing it needs a free slot: `p1: P(b_empty);`. After writing it has created a full slot: `p2: V(b_full);`.

steps.title: Consumer
steps.body: Before reading it needs a full slot: `c1: P(b_full);`. After removing the item it has freed a slot: `c2: V(b_empty);`.

steps.title: Check
steps.body: With b_full = 0 the consumer blocks on an empty buffer; after 100 puts b_empty = 0 and the producer blocks on a full buffer.

pitfalls: Swapping the semaphores (P(b_full) in the producer) — the producer would block forever at start since b_full = 0.
cse-2002-b-68-a.verification: Invariant b_full + b_empty = BUFFSIZE holds between operations.

cse-2002-b-68-b.approach: With several producers (consumers), two can update `first` (`last`) concurrently. Wrap the buffer access and index update in a binary semaphore, taken after the counting wait so no one sleeps while holding it.

steps.title: Race to fix
steps.body: Two producers can both write `buf[first]` before either increments `first`, overwriting an item; likewise two consumers can read the same `buf[last]`.

steps.title: Placement
Why this order
steps.body: P(mutex) comes **after** P(b_empty)/P(b_full). If a producer took mutex first and then blocked on a full buffer, no consumer could get mutex to free a slot — deadlock.

answer.value: `semaphore mutex = 1;` — `P(mutex);` immediately after p1 and c1, `V(mutex);` immediately before p2 and c2.

pitfalls: Putting P(mutex) before P(b_empty) — deadlock when the buffer is full.
cse-2002-b-68-b.verification: At most one process is between P(mutex) and V(mutex), so index updates are serialised; counting semaphores still bound the buffer.

cse-2002-b-69-a.approach: Loop on $(a|b)^*$ at the start state, then nondeterministically guess where the final $abb$ begins and walk a chain of three transitions.

steps.title: States
steps.body: $q_0$: still in $(a|b)^*$; $q_1$: just read the $a$ of the suffix; $q_2$: read $ab$; $q_3$: read $abb$ (accepting).

steps.title: Check
steps.body: $babb$: $q_0\xrightarrow{b}q_0\xrightarrow{a}q_1\xrightarrow{b}q_2\xrightarrow{b}q_3$ — accepted. $abba$ cannot end in $q_3$ since $q_3$ has no outgoing moves.

pitfalls: Adding a self-loop on q3 — that would accept strings like abba.
cse-2002-b-69-a.verification: Accepted strings are exactly those whose last three symbols are a, b, b.

cse-2002-b-69-b.approach: Each DFA state records the longest suffix of the input that is a prefix of $abb$ ($\varepsilon$, $a$, $ab$, $abb$). On each symbol move to the longest such suffix — same as subset construction on the NFA.

steps.title: States
steps.body: $q_0=\{q_0\}$ (matched $\varepsilon$), $q_1=\{q_0,q_1\}$ (matched $a$), $q_2=\{q_0,q_2\}$ (matched $ab$), $q_3=\{q_0,q_3\}$ (matched $abb$, accepting).

steps.title: Transitions
steps.body:
| State | a | b |
|---|---|---|
| $	o q_0$ | $q_1$ | $q_0$ |
| $q_1$ | $q_1$ | $q_2$ |
| $q_2$ | $q_1$ | $q_3$ |
| $*q_3$ | $q_1$ | $q_0$ |

An $a$ always restarts a match ($	o q_1$); a $b$ from $q_3$ leaves suffix $\ldots bbb$, which matches nothing ($	o q_0$).

steps.title: Run on ababb
steps.body: $q_0\xrightarrow{a}q_1\xrightarrow{b}q_2$

steps.title: Mismatch recovery
steps.body: $q_2\xrightarrow{a}q_1$: the third symbol $a$ breaks the partial match $ab$ but starts a new match.

steps.title: Accept
steps.body: $q_1\xrightarrow{b}q_2\xrightarrow{b}q_3$ — input consumed in the accepting state, so $ababb$ is accepted.

pitfalls: Sending $q_2\xrightarrow{a}$ to $q_0$ — loses the fresh $a$ (would reject $ababb$).
Sending $q_3\xrightarrow{b}$ to $q_2$ — $\ldots abbb$ does not end in $ab$.
cse-2002-b-69-b.verification: Subset construction from the NFA gives exactly the four reachable subsets $\{q_0\},\{q_0,q_1\},\{q_0,q_2\},\{q_0,q_3\}$.

cse-2002-b-70-a.approach: The root production is either $E\to E+E$ or $E\to E*E$; each choice forces the rest of the tree, giving exactly two parse trees.

steps.title: Root E → E + E
steps.body: Left $E\Rightarrow i$; right $E\Rightarrow E*E\Rightarrow j*k$. Tree groups as $i+(j*k)$.\n\nLeftmost derivation: $E\Rightarrow E+E\Rightarrow i+E\Rightarrow i+E*E\Rightarrow i+j*E\Rightarrow i+j*k$.

steps.title: Root E → E * E
steps.body: Left $E\Rightarrow E+E\Rightarrow i+j$; right $E\Rightarrow k$. Tree groups as $(i+j)*k$.\n\nLeftmost derivation: $E\Rightarrow E*E\Rightarrow E+E*E\Rightarrow i+E*E\Rightarrow i+j*E\Rightarrow i+j*k$.

steps.title: No others
steps.body: The root must split the string at one of the two operators, and each remaining part ($i$, $j*k$, $i+j$, $k$) has a unique tree. So there are exactly **2** parse trees.

answer.value: Two trees: $E\to E+E$ with the right $E\to E*E$, i.e. $i+(j*k)$; and $E\to E*E$ with the left $E\to E+E$, i.e. $(i+j)*k$.

pitfalls: Writing the leaves as $id$ only — the question asks for the trees of $i+j*k$ (each leaf is $id$ with lexeme $i$, $j$, $k$).
cse-2002-b-70-a.verification: Two distinct leftmost derivations confirm the grammar is ambiguous for this string.

cse-2002-b-70-b.approach: Precedence is encoded by grammar levels (higher-precedence operators derived deeper). Here both operators come from the same non-terminal at the same level.

steps.title: Same level
steps.body: Both $E\to E+E$ and $E\to E*E$ have the same left side and the same shape, so the grammar does not force $*$ below $+$ (or vice versa) in a parse tree.

steps.title: Consequence
steps.body: As part (a) shows, $i+j*k$ can be grouped as $i+(j*k)$ or $(i+j)*k$: **no precedence is defined** — effectively both operators have equal precedence, and associativity is also unspecified.

answer.value: No precedence is defined by the grammar — both `*` and `+` are at the same level (effectively equal precedence), which is why it is ambiguous.

pitfalls: Answering "* is higher" from arithmetic convention — the grammar itself does not enforce it.
cse-2002-b-70-b.verification: Both parse trees from part (a) are valid, so neither operator is forced to bind tighter.

cse-2002-b-70-c.approach: Stratify the grammar: one non-terminal per precedence level, with left recursion for left associativity. The result is unambiguous and LALR(1).

steps.title: Rewrite
steps.body: $$E\to E+T \mid T \qquad T\to T*F \mid F \qquad F\to id$$\n\n$*$ is generated deeper ($T$ level), so it binds tighter than $+$; left recursion makes both left-associative.

steps.title: Effect on i + j * k
steps.body: Only one tree: $E\Rightarrow E+T$, $E\Rightarrow T\Rightarrow F\Rightarrow i$, $T\Rightarrow T*F\Rightarrow j*k$ — the grouping $i+(j*k)$.

steps.title: Alternative
steps.body: Keep the ambiguous grammar but give the LALR generator precedence declarations (e.g. yacc `%left '+'` then `%left '*'`), which resolve the shift/reduce conflicts the same way.

answer.value: Use $E\to E+T\mid T,\ T\to T*F\mid F,\ F\to id$ (or declare `%left '+'` then `%left '*'` so $*$ has higher precedence and both are left-associative).

pitfalls: Right-recursive rules ($E\to T+E$) are also unambiguous but make $+$ right-associative.
cse-2002-b-70-c.verification: The LALR(1) table for the layered grammar has no conflicts (standard expression grammar).
